newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Airlines to hold urgent talks on fuel cost surge.
newsitem.headline: Airlines to hold urgent talks on fuel cost surge.

text.p: Airline officials will meet in two weeks to consider taking possible "concerted action" to counter a 10 per cent fuel cost rise which is eating into profits, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) said on Tuesday.
The crisis talks among IATA's 250 member airlines, set for November 13 in Geneva, take place against the background of crude prices running at five-year highs.

The IATA meeting, officially known as a "tariff coordinating conference", will bring together senior tariff officials who could decide on increases in passenger fares and cargo rates, according to IATA spokesman Tim Goodyear.
The airlines could elect to absorb the added fuel expense -- but it would be at the cost of investing in badly-needed new aircraft, he added.
"They will consider the need for concerted action to counter the increase in the fuel cost burden. It could mean a fare and rate increase," Goodyear told Reuters.
"We don't know what they will decide. They could do nothing or could pass on an increase in fares and rates," he added.
The average worldwide price of fuel paid by IATA members during the first nine months of this year was U.S. 73.9 cents per U.S. gallon, against U.S. 65.2 cents in 1995.
"Fuel costs have been going up pretty steadily this year," Goodyear said. "This is not sudden. It is a creeping crisis."
"Airlines have been hurt economically...If it carries on, a lot of net profit of airlines will disappear," he added.
Internationally scheduled services spend $13 billion a year on aviation fuel, according to the IATA spokesman.
"If the fuel price goes up 10 per cent, that is an extra $1.3 billion compared with airlines profits last year of $5.2 billion," Goodyear said.
IATA members posted $5.2 billion profit last year, or some four per cent profit on operating revenues of some $120 billion, according to the spokesman.

"They need to do better. In order to invest in the newest and best aircraft which are more efficient, less costly, burn relatively less fuel and emit less harmful gases, they need to be considerably more profitable than four per cent," he said.
"If a fuel crisis comes along, they can't absorb it and at the same time invest in new aircraft, which they badly need to do," Goodyear said.
The emergency talks will take place shortly after airline executives attend IATA's annual general meeting November 4-5.

Swissair AG announced on Tuesday that it would raise its cargo rates by 10 U.S. cents per kilo of freight forwarded from November 15, primarily due to the significant rise in jet fuel costs over the last 12 months.
Swissair Cargo said in a statement issued in Zurich that it would continue to follow movements on the jet fuel market and consider future developments in its rate policy.
Over the last year the dollar price for jet fuel has risen roughly 50 percent and since July the price for one gallon of kerosene has risen some 12 percent to 83 cents from 74 cents.
"Market indications point to a continuation of this sharp rise over the medium term," Swissair said.
Other factors, such as higher landing and safety fees and overflight rights, have also affected costs, Swissair added.
